source_document.body:
A veteran truck driver in Georgia has launched a free online platform designed to help truckers find parking , locate roadside repairs, compare diesel prices and access other resources without paying subscription fees.
Shawn Gresham, a 17-year commercial driver and founder of Trucking Life Academy in Dalton, Georgia, said his Trucking Life With Shawn platform currently lists 2,031 truck parking locations across 45 states.
The directory includes 1,882 truck stops, 78 dedicated truck parking lots and 71 hotels that accommodate commercial trucks. It also features 259 listings for truck repair, tire services, roadside assistance and heavy-duty towing, according to Gresham.
“Truckers get nickeled and dimed to death across a hundred different apps: one for parking, one for fuel prices, one for HOS math, one to study for the CDL,” Gresham told FreightWaves. “I built one place, by a trucker, with all of it, free.”
Gresham said the directory has been under development since July and is now being made available to the public. He said 80 listings were added over the past 30 days.
The platform does not display real-time parking availability. Instead, it identifies locations where drivers may park , with listings marked to indicate whether overnight parking has been confirmed or remains unverified.
Drivers can search by state, interstate and exit number, rather than downloading an app or creating an account.
“The directory itself comes from something personal,” Gresham said. “I ran 17 years with a paper truck stop guide on the dash and wrote my own notes all through it.”
He said the online version is designed to recreate that experience on a smartphone, allowing drivers to quickly identify parking locations and roadside services along their routes.
During a demonstration with FreightWaves, Gresham showed how drivers can select a state, interstate and travel direction to find truck stops and parking locations along their route.
A separate repair directory allows drivers to locate towing companies, tire services and other repair providers near interstate exits.
Gresham said the feature was inspired by his own experiences trying to locate assistance after a breakdown.
Instead of searching multiple websites and calling companies that might be dozens of miles away, drivers can identify services near their location and contact them directly through the directory.
The platform also includes a diesel price board that Gresham said is updated daily.
Drivers can compare estimated prices by state, region and city, along with using a calculator to evaluate potential fuel costs.
Gresham, who also works in fuel operations at Rosedale Transport, said he uses diesel pricing information supplied by Love’s Travel Stops to help populate the platform.
“It’s not perfectly average, but it gives you a good idea of what that state’s going for that day,” Gresham said.
He said the information could help drivers and fleets make more informed decisions about where to purchase fuel along their routes.
Gresham is also developing a truck navigation system and trip planner, which he expects to release publicly on New Year’s Eve.
The GPS system is currently being tested by 87 working truck drivers, according to Gresham.
He said the pilot program has allowed developers to identify and correct navigation problems before making the system widely available.
One early issue involved delayed turn notifications, which Gresham said has since been addressed.
The accompanying trip planner is designed to help drivers identify potential stopping locations based on their routes, weather, traffic conditions and remaining available driving hours.
Drivers must manually enter their available hours of service, and Gresham emphasized that the tool is not an electronic logging device or a replacement for federally required hours-of-service records.
The system is intended to identify potential parking locations before drivers exhaust their available driving time.
Gresham said he has intentionally limited access to the GPS pilot while testing continues.
“I didn’t want a brand new driver to use it, and then it did something wrong,” he said.
Drivers interested in participating in the pilot can contact Gresham through the website.
Although the platform’s driver tools are free, Gresham said the website generates revenue through several channels.
Those include sales of his trucking books and guides, affiliate commissions from Truck Parking Club and paid featured listings for businesses such as repair shops.
Gresham said Truck Parking Club is working to integrate its reservable parking locations into his directory, allowing drivers to access paid parking options through the platform.
He receives affiliate compensation when users book qualifying parking through the referral arrangement.
Gresham said drivers can continue using the free parking directory without purchasing a reservation.
The platform also includes CDL practice tests, educational articles, study guides and a sleeper berth split calculator intended to help drivers understand hours-of-service calculations.
He said the goal is to consolidate resources that truckers might otherwise access through multiple websites or subscription services.
“Drivers never pay, and they never will,” Gresham said of the platform’s driver tools.
The online platform follows Gresham’s efforts to establish Trucking Life Academy, a CDL training school in Dalton built with equipment and other contributions from drivers and businesses.
The academy is scheduled to open this month, pending final state approval.
Gresham previously told FreightWaves that he established the school in response to concerns about the quality of CDL training and the preparation of new commercial drivers.
The school plans to limit classes to six students and initially offer training over eight weekends.
The new online platform expands that effort beyond prospective CDL holders to drivers already working in the trucking industry.
Gresham said the parking directory is now publicly accessible, although he does not yet have meaningful usage figures because the service is newly launched.
He said working drivers can submit additional parking locations and corrections, which he reviews before publishing.
“Parking is a huge problem,” he said. “I just want truckers using it.”
Why it matters: The platform aims to give truckers easier access to parking and operational information without requiring multiple paid subscriptions, although its parking directory does not provide live space availability.

Canadian EV customers are delaying buying decisions while they wait for more Chinese EVs to reach their shores, according to a new survey, suggesting widespread awareness of China’s EV dominance is causing EV buyers to ignore Western automakers’ offerings entirely.
The survey was commissioned by Clean Energy Canada , and shows that Canadian interest in EVs is slowly ticking up, with nearly half of them inclined, likely or certain to buy an EV as their next vehicle.
But more interestingly, among potential EV buyers, there’s one big stumbling block: China.
Originally, Canada had the same tariff on Chinese EVs that the USA had, a 100% tariff implemented ( unwisely ) by President Biden. As trade partners with the US and with a heavily intermeshed auto industry (given Detroit is literally a stone’s throw away from Canada), Canada thought it would be wise to maintain a united front on auto tariffs.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
But then, idiocy happened . The squatter in the US White House put tariffs on Canada leading to immediate job losses , and repeatedly threatened its sovereignty. Now, the US’ relationship with Canada is strained, and Canada is looking towards the rest of the world for allies.
At the same time, China saw an opportunity, and decided to put a tariff on Canadian canola . This was a big deal for farmers in the center of the country, and led to the somewhat unexpected effect of the most conservative, oil-loving Canadian provinces lobbying the Canadian government to drop tariffs on Chinese EVs and allow them into the country, in exchange for China dropping canola tariffs.
Now, China and Canada have an agreement which will allow 49,000 Chinese EVs into the country per year, and the first have started to arrive .
But so far, there aren’t actually a ton of Chinese EV models available in Canada yet. Companies are spinning up their distribution networks, but everything is still in progress. Canada is actually nowhere near selling out this year’s 49k quota, with only about 16k Chinese EVs imported total.
Some brands, like Tesla, have already hit their quota allocation , because they already had distribution networks built up. Other brands are lagging. So there aren’t that many models available, and more are expected to hit shores next year.
This has led to a situation where Canadian buyers know that a wave of high-tech, new, reasonably priced EVs are just around the corner (although they are perhaps overestimating how cheap those EVs will be, as prices will be higher in Canada than in China). And where the type of cars they currently have access to in North America are largely from Western brands that have spent this year lobbying against EVs and canceling models . Or, perhaps worse, brands that are associated with the US, which are subject to significantly more negative public opinion in Canada than ever before.
So, Canadian EV buyers don’t want to buy American cars, and know Chinese EVs are coming, and are higher tech and cheaper than European and Japanese EVs.
This all led to the interesting survey result in question. Of the 48% of Canadians surveyed who said they were likely to buy an EV for their next vehicle, 42% said they wanted to “wait for more Chinese EVs to become available.”
So, these are Canadians who already want an EV, and are ready to buy one – at least the next time they buy a car. But instead of getting one, at a time when gas prices are at historic highs (due to, uh, the same aforementioned idiocy), they’re waiting until they see more Chinese cars.
This is a massive condemnation of everything the West has to offer in the electric space right now. In the past, it was thought that Western buyers might be skeptical of Chinese brands, thinking them to be lower quality, as has been the stereotype in the West for a long time.
But now, that dynamic has flipped on its head – Canadians are refusing the options available to them now, and waiting for Chinese options to become available, expecting them to be superior than the traditional options that have been available to them.
And given that it’s taking time for Chinese brands to establish their networks and ship cars Canada, that means a lot of Canadian buyers are twiddling their thumbs right now.
It’s an interesting situation, given most other countries already have access to Chinese EVs, and they’re selling well in those countries. And it perhaps offers us a view to what might happen to the US auto industry, if there’s ever a sniff that Chinese EVs might come here (which, inevitably, in the long term, I am sure they will).
With US automakers so far behind on electrification, and constantly lobbying to fall even further behind , it doesn’t feel like the gap is going to get any smaller. Eventually, Americans will see that the rest of the world, including their two closest neighbors, are getting access to cheap, efficient EVs that don’t give them the anxiety of supporting the most evil industry in the history of the world to fuel. Eventually, they’ll get tired of spending so much for so little , when everyone else gets great cars for cheap.

There are a few moves within American automakers to try to compete , but it remains to be seen if that’s too little or too late. China has released literally thousands of new EV models, with cutthroat competition driving prices down and quality up.
We do not see that sort of competition happening in the US, especially after republicans sent so many EV jobs to China . And being given the safety blanket of tariffs won’t encourage harsher competition , it will just lull automakers into a false sense of security . The only way to catch a moving target that’s in front of you is to move faster than them, and US automakers simply are not doing that right now.
But US consumers will figure it out eventually. And Canada’s EV buyers are a signal of what’s to come.

More than 40 kilograms of cocaine traveled from California to Florida aboard a commercial truck without the carrier’s knowledge. Investigators intercepted the shipment as suspects began unpacking a pallet containing the drugs. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced October 13 that Operation Icebreaker uncovered a trafficking network spanning three South Florida counties. Authorities charged 25 individuals in connection with the operation.
Investigators seized approximately 45.5 kilograms of cocaine during the operation. Uthmeier announced the takedown following enforcement operations across Palm Beach, Broward and St. Lucie counties. Officers also recovered fentanyl, methamphetamine, prescription pills and firearms.
How cocaine moved through commercial freight
According to the Attorney General’s announcement, traffickers concealed multi- kilogram quantities of cocaine aboard commercial trucks. The organization relied on legitimate carriers that authorities described as unaware of the illegal cargo. Investigators identified Ariel Fernandez-Alonso as a major supplier who reportedly claimed receiving 50 to 60 kilograms every 15 days. Detectives intercepted one delivery as Fernandez-Alonso and associates began unloading the shipment.
Authorities have not confirmed whether the intercepted pallet traveled through a truckload or less-than-truckload network. Investigators have not identified the shipper, consignee, freight broker or carrier. Specific pickup and delivery locations also remain undisclosed. Court records provide no additional details about the shipment arrangements.
Previous FreightWaves reporting has documented other drug trafficking operations involving commercial transportation. One investigation uncovered a $139 million trafficking operation involving broker-style arrangements with knowing drivers. Another case involved $6 million in cocaine concealed beneath a semi-trailer’s floor near the Canadian border.
Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office narcotics detectives began investigating suspicious social media activity in March 2026. A 162-page arrest warrant affidavit details undercover purchases, court-authorized wiretaps and surveillance of suspected distributors. Detectives identified Kenny Charles as a primary supplier to Richard Paterniti during the operation. The filing does not explain how investigators first identified the intercepted California shipment.
Investigators identify trafficking network across three counties
Authorities executed more than 20 search warrants during coordinated enforcement operations. Prosecutors charged 25 individuals, including Fernandez-Alonso, Paterniti, Charles, Craig Benard, Jerri Kitzelman and Jerry Salerno. Charges include drug trafficking, racketeering conspiracy and unlawful use of communication devices. All defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
Why it matters
Legitimate trucking companies can unknowingly transport illegal cargo when traffickers exploit commercial freight networks. The case highlights the importance of shipper verification, accurate cargo documentation and maintaining control throughout the transportation process.

Tesla had 103 job openings with Semi in the title posted at its Sparks, Nevada, truck plant as of Oct. 16, according to Tesla’s careers site . The listings come three weeks after the plant started high-volume Semi production on Sept. 24.
The hiring is for a 1.7-million-square-foot factory designed to build 50,000 trucks a year, as fleets line up orders for a truck Tesla first showed in 2017. Tesla has not said how many Semis the plant is building now. Before the dedicated line opened, the Semi fleet numbered just under 200 pilot trucks, delivered to customers including DHL, PepsiCo and US Foods.
Drayage carrier IMC Logistics ordere d 50 Semis this month, following WattEV’s 370-t r uck order in May. Tesla was also named lead manufacturer on a 2,500-truck order through the ZET SCALE alliance in September, though the alliance did not say how many of those trucks will be Semis.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk told analysts in July, “We have started production with the Tesla semi-truck.” The company’s second-quarter shareholder update said production was expected to begin later in the year .
Semi openings span assembly to dispatch
The Semi listings include quality technicians for stamping, body-in-white and powertrain; equipment maintenance technicians for general assembly and the drivetrain; and a CDL driver, a dispatcher and an endurance fleet driver.
Several are night-shift roles, including a battery production supervisor, associate production managers and stamping quality technicians. Tesla is also hiring construction staff for the Semi site, from a pipefitter to an electrical superintendent.
The Semi roles are part of a larger list: Tesla’s site showed 490 openings in Sparks, 301 of them in manufacturing. The company’s Sparks listings on Indeed include production roles on battery, Powerwall, drive unit and LFP cell lines.
Semi service and charging build out beyond Nevada
Another 66 Semi postings sit outside Sparks. In the U.S., Tesla is hiring Semi service managers, supervisors and technical instructors in 11 cities, including Laredo, Texas; Elizabeth, New Jersey; and Chicago.
On the charging side, Pilot and Tesla opened their first Megacharger site in Ellabell, Georgia, Oct. 8, with 12 more under construction.
Tesla is also hiring for the Semi in Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium and the U.K., where it is targeting customer deliveries by the end of 2027 . Postings there include service technicians in Berlin, Düsseldorf and Lyon, France.
The first European trucks will come from Nevada. “We’ve got ample capacity to support our initial wave,” Dan Priestley, who leads the Semi program, said in a September keynote at IAA Transportation in Hannover, Germany.
Output figures remain undisclosed
Tesla’s third-quarter delivery report on Oct. 2 did not mention the Semi, and the company has not disclosed pricing. It reports quarterly results after the market closes Oct. 21.
Semi postings are down from the spring even as Tesla’s overall Nevada postings rose. Stocktwits counted 146 Semi roles among nearly 471 full-time Nevada jobs on Tesla’s site in April, though it did not say how it identified Semi roles. On Oct. 16, the site listed 103 Semi-titled roles and 537 full-time Nevada openings.
Priestley has also said “Tesla is not a heavy truck company yet,” FreightWaves reported in its coverage of the Sept. 24 inauguration.
Why it matters: Tesla is staffing a Nevada plant built for 50,000 trucks a year as IMC, WattEV and ZET SCALE orders arrive. It has not said how many Semis the plant builds today, and its Oct. 21 results are the next chance to find out.

Keystone's 2027 Outback Is Here With a New Layout – the 221Frost Is All for Adventurous Families
26 photos
Photo: Camping World | YouTube Screenshot
With 2027, travel trailer and camper manufacturers have begun to show off the goodies of next year, and one brand that has been in the spotlight quite a bit lately is Keystone RV. Well, for 2027, they’ve unveiled a new floorplan for the Outback class, this brand’s off-road-loving lineup. Mind you, this one is ready to meet the needs of countless adventurers out there.
For 2027, Keystone RV has added two new floorplans to their Outback lineage, one of which is officially the smallest of the class: the 221Frost. However, “smallest” is only relative considering that the Outback has always been known as a beefy and equipped class of campers.
Furthermore, they are this brand’s off-road-capable monsters, equipped with a Curt Touring Coil suspension that grants us access to nothing other than independent action for each of the four wheels that carry this shell and all its goodies to wherever it is you want to go. Once you arrive at that X on your map, you’ll be able to tap into so many features, comforts, and supplies, that you may end up feeling at home, and that’s kind of the idea .
Photo: Camping World | YouTube Screenshot Keep in mind that Keystone does build these babies with quite the shell, but according to owners and forums, they aren’t truly four-season ready, and some parts are still exposed and can cause problems in freezing environments.
You’ll need to make some modifications to truly stay out there for as long as possible and be ready to burn quite the amount of gas and/or fuel.
After making a little plot of land nearly 27 feet (8.3 m) long, hook up to shore power or draw juice from your batteries, engage the slide-out and awning along the camping side, and before long, you and the gang are unloading goodies gathering firewood, and setting up the campsite.
What I liked most about the exterior of the 221Frost is the presence of an outdoor kitchen ready with a griddle and a fridge, the latter being essential so that you don’t drag dirt into your unit just to grab a drink. It doesn’t sound like a big deal until the campsite starts to get a bit dusty, possibly muddy.
Photo: Lippert While you can hop into the camper via the main entrance, like any normal human being out there, there is another way in, and frankly, it's a trick that also allows us to see part of this RV’s versatility .
At the very rear of the 221Frost, Keystone added another door, well, almost a door; it’s actually a hatch that invites us to load gear into this camper. Kayaks will fit through this door, and so will bicycles and e-bikes. Heck, some electric pit and dirt bikes will too, but you will need some help loading it in.
I can, however, see this feature as being used by the kids frequently, especially if they’re playing tag or hide and seek, so be ready for some extra use. Maybe add a little step at the rear to help keep things safe.
This little cargo and toy garage does utilize the space provided by the lower double bunk that is located on this side of the camper, but that does still leave the upper bunk intact, so two kids still have a place to rest at night. Check out the little storage options integrated into the steps that lead the kids to the upper bedding area.
In terms of sleeping accommodations, we have these two bunks, but at the opposite end of the layout, under the front cap, Keystone added a Murphy bed that is to be accessed at night. During the day, this section lies in wait with a couch and does free up a bit of the floor for moving around.
Photo: Camping World | YouTube Screenshot More sleeping arrangements are found at the dinette. The host of the video below – a big thank you goes out to Camping World for the amazing walk-through - talks about this area of the camper and mentions that is a telescopic leg underneath the table, hinting that this feature can indeed take the shape of a bed when needed.
One thing to jot down in your mental journal is that, unlike other Outback units, this one doesn’t include the atrium windows in the ceiling of the slide, so seeing the stars at night is to be enjoyed by whomever has the window seat, so to speak.
Along the camping side of the 221Frost, Keystone adds the kitchen first, ready with a countertop that’s also a bar-like area, three-burner gas top, a deep-bowl sink, residential fridge/freezer, three-in-one oven, and more than enough storage options.
Take note that the TV is also located above the bar-top and does include a swivel function that allows us to point it toward any section of the camper.
Photo: Camping World | YouTube Screenshot The bathroom is also an interesting one, and since the rear is occupied by the bunks, Keystone was forced to place the toilet right next to the door, and just before the shower; you have to step past the toilet to enter the stall. It is a three-piece dry bath, though.
What I want to mention about the shower is that there’s ample headroom for taller users too. Check out the clip below for a more visual representation of what that means.
Clearly, the rest of this bad boy is equipped with all the systems we need to stay warm or cool, have power whenever we need it, and even tap into free juice from the sun, to name a few, but to go through everything would mean we’d be here until the cows come home.
However, a couple of very important traits include the tempered glass entrance door, rack and pinion slide, and the accessory hitch at the rear, not to mention the spare tire mount. Controls over all systems are located inside and by the door.
Photo: Camping World | YouTube Screenshot Be sure to dive in deeper into the composite and aluminum shell Keystone uses to give life to this rolling and family ready RV and how they manage a dry weight of as little as 6,110 lbs (2,771 kg). GVWR stands at 8,200 lbs (3,720 kg), so a bit over 2,000 lbs (907 kg) of cargo-carrying capacity. Of course, you never want to max out your GVWR and extra features and options also occupy some of this number.
Speaking of numbers, dealers are letting the 221Frost go for as low as the $55K (€49K) range, but most are sitting around $60K. Find one, check it out, and haggle with the dealer to drop the price.

2026 Paris Motor Show • Chinese Brand AITO Plans 2027 European Launch
Scott Sets Its Sights on "SUV" Rides and Delivers E-Ville Step-Though E-Bike With Full Suspension
17 photos
Photo: Scott Sports Global
Since 1958, the name Scott has been spotted on sporting gear and goods, and ever since 1992, that same name could be seen on bicycles. Recently, Scott dropped what they feel is the perfect urban e-bike. I mean, why launch a new model if it isn’t the peak of what you can achieve as a brand?
It’s called the E-Ville, and while its name can be read as “evil,” there’s nothing evil about it. On the contrary; the E-Ville is all about being one of the most comfortable e-bikes the industry can muster, and we’re here to find out what the heck is going on.
First and foremost, the E-Ville is designed as an urban solution , but, with a very big catch: the ability to also break away from the tarmac and hit up some actual trails. We’re looking at a full-suspension e-bike, one that’s built around a step-through frame; it’s one of the most odd-ball configurations that the cycling industry spits out. Scott considers this one an SUV, meeting a particular segment of cycling that is growing.
Photo: Scott Sports Global People are looking for bikes that eliminate the need for multiples in order to tackle particular terrains, and while the hardtail MTB has been the called-upon frame style that we use for a do-it-all bike, recent industry trends have seen the development of the SUV bicycle.
These options differ from brand to brand, but usually, an SUV is signaled by a full-suspension frame, cargo-carrying abilities, and comfort that’s meant to keep you in the saddle for as long as possible, granting us access to long rides to the edge of town and a bit beyond.
But, what I can’t shake is that most e-bike SUVs are built with a step-through frame, and if I may, all I see when I look at one of these rides is my grandma hitting up some trails, decked out to the teeth with safety gear, and carrying freshly baked bread and juice on that cargo rack; mind the eggs .
Speaking of cargo, the E-Ville can also be adapted with a cargo trailer, turning this electrified machine into a source of transportation for the entire family.
Photo: Scott Sports Global Helping us haul all that extra baggage is none other than Bosch, supplying the motor mounted into the BB of this bike. While there are two versions available, both are rocking a Performance Line CX motor with 100 Nm (74 lb-ft) of peak torque.
That’s more than enough to tackle ups and downs out there and once coupled with a Shimano CUES with 10 or 11 speeds, we’re set, and may even end up riding the E-Ville without electric assistance sometimes.
In the range department, the E-Ville 10, the more expensive of the two, features an 800 Wh PowerTube, granting us access to a reported 150 km (93 miles) of ride time. The E-Ville 20, the least expensive of the two offers 130 km (81 miles), but both can carry range extenders, so this isn’t the limit here. Since the packs are removable, we can also look into another and double our ride times.
Photo: Scott Sports Global On the comfort side of things, I mentioned that the E-Ville is built with a full suspension frame, and depending on the version, we either find an SR Suntour (20 with 100 mm of travel) or RockShox (10 with 120 mm of travel), and at the rear, SR Suntour handles the action on both frames.
Extra comfort for this lineup is accessed with a dropper post, which also helps us clear the saddle when riding rougher terrain, an adjustable stem, and the tires with 60 mm of cross-section, or around 2.35 inches. That’s a cross-section that’s as wide as MTB tires and the tread looks ready for a light trail too.
With handlebars, the cargo rack, fenders, and lights at the front and rear, we’re granted access to an e-bike that weighs around 69 lbs (31.3 kg) no matter the version you choose, so they definitely aren’t the lightest out there, which can be seen as a drawback and benefit.
Photo: Scott Sports Global The drawback is the actual weight, making it difficult to take up a flight of stairs, and the benefit is a solid stance and center of gravity while riding. The latter also plays into carrying cargo.
As for pricing, it will depend greatly on where you are in the world, with some countries dropping the 10 for as much as €5,300 and €4,600 for the 20, placing the E-Ville into the “up there” category in terms of pricing and accessibility. Quite a bit of cash, but for quite a whole lot of e-bike.
The ultimate question is whether or not this one is for you, and the best way to find the answer is to seek an E-Ville in a shop near you, take it out for a spin, and understand why SUVs are being focused on in terms of a current trend that manufacturers are fulfilling.
Keep in mind that US riders aren’t yet able to acquire this one; that may change.

At University College London (UCL), a group of students applauded when a small supercomputer switched on.
To be fair, they’d just helped assemble it.
We’d handed out cables, invited people to connect the components and encouraged questions. Why did that cable go into this port? What was the difference between Ethernet and Omni-Path? How did the nodes connect to one another?
It was the first stop of our Sustainable Reality HPC & AI Roadshow , hosted in collaboration with UCL and STEP-UP. Over the following week, we travelled to Queen’s University Belfast, Cardiff University, and the University of York: different locations, different participants, but the same enthusiasm for getting hands-on with HPC hardware.
Students examine the cabling at UCL (Image courtesy Cristin Merritt)
Across four events in eight days, Alces Flight and our university partners welcomed 181 participants, including 122 who said this would be their first experience working with HPC.
We weren’t trying to create experts in a day. We wanted people to encounter a real system, discover what interested them and find opportunities to continue.
A Cluster with Another Job to Do
The hardware at the centre of Sustainable Reality had already completed its original role in research computing. Now it had another purpose: introducing people to the infrastructure behind HPC.
We brought genuine cluster components into the room, handed out cables and invited participants to help put everything together. Many were encountering this equipment for the first time. Their questions often started with the basics, but those basics can lead in interesting directions.
Why does a particular cable connect to a particular port? Follow that question far enough, and you’re discussing network architecture and topology. What’s the difference between Ethernet and Omni-Path? That opens questions about bandwidth, latency, and the role of high-performance interconnects. At one location, engineers brought their own interest in photonics into the conversation.
We weren’t expecting anyone to master these subjects in a morning. We wanted to give them a starting point, and the confidence to keep asking questions.
The hardware itself offered a lesson in sustainability. Its original deployment had ended, but its usefulness hadn’t. It had found a new role helping people understand the systems that support research.
A cluster for the competition (Image courtesy Cristin Merritt )
A supercomputer is a record of decisions, from its architecture and networking to the software it runs and the resources it consumes. Giving people the chance to explore the hardware is one way to begin making those decisions visible.
From First Job to Experimentation
After the physical build, participants connected to a separately prepared computing environment, learned basic Linux and Slurm commands, and submitted their first jobs.
I’d initially worried we’d packed too much into the day. At UCL, where we could invite students aged 16 and up, our youngest participants needed most of the allotted time. At the university locations, however, once people successfully submitted a sample job, many were ready to explore independently.
The afternoon activity involved generating images from the Mandelbrot Set. We provided starting regions and instructions, then encouraged people to experiment.
We’d designed the workload for CPUs. Naturally, someone decided to try the GPU.
Others investigated Linux commands, edited job scripts, modified Python, or experimented with colours and coordinates. I watched one participant explain the mathematics behind the Mandelbrot calculation to another.
Those experiments could lead to bigger questions about workload characteristics, parallelism, resource scheduling, and how software uses different hardware. But the participants didn’t need to understand all of that to begin exploring.
Cardiff University during the competition (Image courtesy Cristin Merritt)
Our portable WiFi equipment could support only around 30 to 35 connections, so people worked together around tables. Someone might run a job while others investigated commands, code or possible changes.
And they weren’t working alone. Our Alces team was joined by departmental leaders and research computing specialists from each host institution, including RSEs who helped participants through the exercises and supported their increasingly varied questions.
We provided the starting point. The participants found plenty of directions to go next.
More Than One Route into HPC
Through my work on the SC Conference Series Women’s History Month project , I’ve spent years hearing how people found their way into research computing.
One thing has become clear: Nobody arrives on the same bus.
Some come through computer science or engineering. Others through mathematics, physics, biology or an unexpected research project. That’s why we deliberately welcomed people from different academic backgrounds and didn’t require prior HPC experience.
We also wanted to demonstrate that nobody in HPC knows everything. Research computing depends on different expertise working together, from infrastructure and networking to scientific applications, research software and operations.
That variety was evident throughout the Roadshow. Some participants gravitated toward hardware; others toward mathematics or programming. What caught one person’s attention wasn’t necessarily what interested the person sitting beside them. And that was the whole point.
An Invitation to Continue
We designed Sustainable Reality as a pathway into opportunities already available across the HPC community.
A York student discussing the Mandelbrot set (Image courtesy Cristin Merritt)
Two particular ambitions were to help form or strengthen teams for the CIUK Student Cluster Challenge and to work towards a collective Art of HPC submission in 2027 using images participants created. We also shared information about student programmes, volunteering and other ways to get involved.
With SC26 approaching and the Student Cluster Competition celebrating its twentieth anniversary, our community has created many opportunities worth celebrating. But what happens before someone feels ready to participate?
An introductory event won’t teach everything, and we don’t yet know how many Roadshow participants will pursue further opportunities. We observed that with real infrastructure, enough guidance to get started, and room to experiment, people found questions worth investigating on their own.
Sustainable research computing depends on more than efficient systems and responsible resource use. It also needs people with the knowledge and curiosity to build, operate and improve what comes next. Our cluster has already supported research. Now it’s helping people discover the field behind it.
That’s a second life worth celebrating.
Interested in helping us create more opportunities like Sustainable Reality? We’re always keen to connect with universities, research computing teams and others across the HPC community who would like to get involved. Please email me at [email protected] to start a conversation.
About the author: Cristin Merritt leads Communications and Partner Ecosystems at Alces Flight , where her work focuses on connecting people, ideas and opportunities across the HPC community.
Acknowledgements: With thanks to the Alces and ConcertIM teams, and our collaborators at University College London and STEP-UP, Queen’s University Belfast, Cardiff University and the University of York, whose expertise, enthusiasm and support made the Sustainable Reality HPC & AI Roadshow possible.

Texas Car Hunter Finds 1971 Challenger 340 Six-Pack Ragtop in West Virginia, It's Full of Options
40 photos
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins
When an automotive treasure hunter from Texas rolls into a town with a population of less than 100 people in West Virginia, you know heavy Detroit iron is about to see daylight. Bruceton Mills, West Virginia, is a place that should be marked with an X on a pirate’s map, because that’s where the treasure had been hiding since 2007. A 1971 Dodge Challenger convertible 340 Six-Pack, tucked inside a dark storage unit, from a family ownership of 34 years.
A 1971 Challenger convertible WHAT ? 340 Six-Pack. As in “three two-barrel carbs” siting atop the most wolverine motor ChryCo ever had the audacity of letting loose on the street. And, of course, Dodge advertised it accordingly for 1971, proudly announcing the T/A for the model year in the fall of 1970.
That was, of course, before they had a change of heart/mind, and dropped the model entirely, too late for the printed brochures to be halted from distribution. But that’s about all there was to the Six-Pack small-block saga for the 1971 model year: a printed “what if.” Which, of course, prompted a lot of gearheads to set things right, and build what Chrysler refused to.
Bill grew up in a household where Mopar muscle was a way of life. Back in the early 1970s, his parents daily-drove a triple-black 1970 Challenger R/T 440 convertible until the 1973 oil embargo turned commuting into a financial nightmare and forced a sale. Talk about cool dads, huh?
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins Determined to recapture that open-air magic, Bill's father tracked down this 1971 Challenger drop-top around 1992 after it came out of Rockville, Maryland, near Washington, D.C. Prior to 1992, a previous Maryland owner yanked the factory 318-cubic-inch V8 and dropped in a date-coded 1971 340-cubic-inch V8 topped with a Six-Pack setup of three two-barrel carburetors.
Bill's dad added a dual-scoop R/T hood, R/T rear valance, quad-exhaust tips, and a 150-mph Rallye instrument cluster. A windshield sticker proves it attended the 2007 Carlisle All-Chrysler Nationals before a 2015 stroke sidelined Bill's father - and the car. Come 2026, and guess who crashes the party? Dennis Collins, because Texas is big enough for all sorts of E-body ragtops, particularly one-of-nones like this amazing example .
The real surprise, though, came back home, once the car got a proper inspection from Alex Bohling, the designated wrencher who was probably still a rugrat when this car was last driven. Which didn’t prevent him from becoming a very skilled mechanic and a dedicated car nut who immediately noticed something Dennis took for granted, or discarded altogether.
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins In the dim West Virginia storage bay, Collins admittedly got caught speeding, assuming the convertible was originally yellow and pieced together with aftermarket goodies. Back in Texas after its 19-year slumber, the car was raised on a lift, and delivered a plot twist. The unpatched floor pans still wore factory undercoating, only the replacement R/T hood had yellow overspray, and the fender tag was completely packed with factory codes.
Built on December 1, 1970, this US-spec convertible left the factory in Bright Red with a black power top, black leather bucket seats, center console, air conditioning, a 26-inch radiator, dual chrome racing mirrors, a trunk rack, and black longitudinal stripes. Sitting on Firestone Firehawk Indy 500 tires and wired with a vintage Excalibur alarm, the 340 Six-Pack fired right up on auxiliary fuel supply. The one-of-none machine is back in action, almost 56 years after it rolled off the line.
After a brief 1959 cameo as the Coronet-based Dodge Silver Challenger, the true E-body pony car debuted for the 1970 model year . It was the only completely new car for that season – not from Dodge, not from Chrysler, from anyone in Detroit. The moniker spanned three distinct generations: the 1970 to 1974 original, the 1978 to 1983 Mitsubishi-built subcompact coupe, and the 2008 to 2023 retro brawler (fingers crossed for a comeback).
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins Across its five-year first-generation run, Dodge sold 165,437 Challengers in the United States, or 169,021 counting Canadian and export deliveries. After launching with 76,935 cars in 1970, domestic output fell to 26,299 units in 1971, out of 29,883 built worldwide, before logging 22,919 in 1972, 27,930 in 1973, and 11,354 in 1974. Convertibles survived just two seasons, totaling 3,884 US sales in 1970 and 1,857 in 1971.
Why did sales crater in 1971? Blame skyrocketing insurance rates and the federal Clean Air Act, which forced Detroit to lower compression ratios for low-lead fuel. Dodge axed the Challenger T/A, dropped the R/T convertible after building 963 in 1970, and eliminated the four-barrel 440 Magnum V8. To keep the hardtop-only R/T accessible, Dodge added the high-revving 275-hp 340-cubic-inch four-barrel V8 to the R/T roster, attracting 1,078 buyers in 1971.
Buyers paired 3- and 4-speed manuals, or a 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic gearbox with the 125-hp 198-cubic-inch and 145-hp 225-cubic-inch Slant-Sixes, the 230-hp 318-cubic-inch V8, or the 275-hp 340-cubic-inch V8.
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins Compression cuts trimmed the two-barrel 383-cubic-inch V8 by 15 hp to 275 hp, the four-barrel 383 Magnum by 35 hp to 300 hp, and the 440-cubic-inch Six-Pack by 5 hp to 385 hp, while the 426-cubic-inch Hemi kept all 425 gross hp.
Breaking down the 1971 model year by body style and trim reveals how scarce open-top E-bodies truly are. Of the 26,299 US-market Challengers, hardtops accounted for 20,628 domestic units, split between 1,672 6-cylinder cars and 18,956 V8s, alongside 3,814 R/T hardtops, including 47 Hemis. Because Dodge canceled the R/T convertible for 1971, the 440 Six-Pack and 426 Hemi never came in 1971 factory ragtops.
That leaves just 1,857 US-spec convertibles for 1971, comprising 83 Slant-Six droptops and 1,774 V8s, including 50 Indy 500 Pace Cars. Drilling down by engine, 167 buyers ordered the top-dog four-barrel 383 V8, with 126 automatics and 41 4-speeds, while 127 chose the two-barrel 383 and 176 picked the 340. Bill's car belongs to the 1,323 318-cubic-inch V8 convertibles, and its 3-speed automatic isolates it to 1,230 units.
While the remaining 93 manual-shift 318 convertibles, split into 74 3-speeds and 19 4-speeds, are statistical ghosts, pairing this 1-of-1,230 automatic ragtop with factory Bright Red paint, air conditioning, leather buckets, and side stripes creates a unicorn. Add the screaming 340 Six-Pack under the hood, plus the front chin spoilers and longitudinal stripes Collins plans to install, and this West Virginia is bound to be the talk of any cars and coffee it will attend.

AI startup Evos raised $9 million in pre-seed funding to develop autonomous software operators for small and midsized industrial businesses, including freight brokerages, the company announced Wednesday.
This comes as the company looks to automate routine work without requiring businesses to replace their existing software.
The round was co-led by Uncork Capital and Field Ventures, with participation from Crosslink Capital, Utopia Capital Management, Sandwith Ventures and angel investors.
Evos said it surpassed $1 million in annual recurring revenue four weeks after launching. The company did not disclose its valuation or the number of customers using its platform.
How it works
Evos is developing AI operators that learn how employees make decisions and carry out specific business functions within a company’s existing systems. Rather than requiring employees to prompt an AI tool for every task, the operators are designed to manage an assigned function independently once their decisions consistently match those of experienced workers.
The approach targets smaller industrial businesses where operational knowledge often rests with experienced employees rather than documented procedures. Evos said its operators learn from employees’ behavior and decisions, with the goal of reproducing their work before taking on tasks autonomously.
“The most capable system in many of these businesses is the person who has been there 20 years, and what they know has never been written down,” said Urav Shah, founder and CEO of Evos.
According to the company’s announcement, 99.3% of U.S. motor carriers operate fewer than 100 trucks, while 93% of U.S. manufacturers have fewer than 100 employees. Evos argues that these businesses need automation that does not require extensive technical resources or lengthy implementation projects.
“The platform is fully self-serve: work that would take a consultant or an implementation partner 9 to 18 months to deliver, an Evos operator takes on in 24 hours from discovery to deployment,” the company said.
One freight brokerage, MyFreightWorld, is using an Evos operator to audit less-than-truckload (LTL) carrier invoices against its transportation management system . Evos said the operator made nearly 3,500 audit decisions over two months with 97% accuracy and identified billing discrepancies valued at more than $600,000 over the most recent five-week period. The $600,000 represents the value of discrepancies identified between invoices involving MyFreightWorld and its end customers, rather than money recovered or savings realized, Evos noted. The company did not explain how it calculated the 97% accuracy rate or specify the sample used to measure performance.
Broader context
LTL invoice audits can uncover billing errors involving accessorial fees, fuel surcharges and freight classifications.
A 2024 analysis by AFS Logistics illustrates the volume of discrepancies that can arise in LTL billing. The company found 11,881 errors in a review of nearly 250,000 invoices. Inaccurate accessorial charges accounted for 42.8% of the errors, followed by fuel surcharges at 14.4% and freight misclassification at 12.3%. The findings reflect AFS’s review rather than the entire LTL market.
The startup’s approach comes as logistics companies continue to seek measurable returns from AI investments. A Boston Consulting Group report published in August 2026 found that only 13% of executives surveyed at 30 leading global logistics companies said AI was delivering measurable financial results, despite two-thirds of respondents reporting a dedicated AI budget and strategy. The findings highlight the gap between investing in AI and translating that investment into measurable business results.
For smaller operators, the cost and complexity of implementation can also determine whether automation is practical. Evos is betting that software capable of learning established workflows and executing tasks within existing systems can lower those barriers.
Why this matters
AI startups are increasingly targeting routine logistics work, but proving that automation delivers measurable financial results remains a challenge. Evos’ work with MyFreightWorld offers a specific example of how AI operators could be used in freight brokerage operations, though the startup has not disclosed how much money the technology has recovered or independently verified its reported accuracy rate.

Danny Keating, an attorney who was one of the masterminds of the Louisiana staged accident scam, was sentenced Thursday to 32 months in federal prison.
Keating’s sentence will be followed by three years of supervised release. He also must pay $657,405.34 in restitution.
Keating was one of the most significant participants in what prosecutors in the office of the U.S. Attorney for Eastern Louisiana dubbed “Operation Sideswipe,” the intentional collisions in the New Orleans area between cars full of participants in the scheme and other vehicles that were usually tractor trailers.
Keating pleaded guilty in June 2021. He is the only attorney involved in the case to cop a plea.
He has been cooperating with prosecutors since then and was a key witness in the successful prosecution of fellow attorneys Vanessa Motta and Jason Giles, who were convicted in March for their roles in the scam. They await sentencing, as earlier sentencing dates were delayed with no new ones set as the two sides work through various motions.
Keating did not testify in the recent mixed bag verdict of several people charged in the murder of Cornelius Garrison , who also had agreed to cooperate with federal prosecutors in 2020 after he pleaded guilty. Garrison was gunned down in his home soon after. The key murder charges in that case ended up in a hung jury with no new trial scheduled, though there were other convictions.
During the interim between his guilty plea and this week, Keating’s sentencing was frequently scheduled and then delayed before finally occurring Thursday.
According to reporting about the sentencing by NOLA.COM , the online successor to the New Orleans Times Picayune, Keating’s attorney Brian Capitelli had asked U.S. District Court Judge Nanette Brown to sentence Keating to probation, citing Keating’s cooperation with the investigation and the fact that he is in poor health.
Keating not only didn’t get that; he also got more than the two years prosecutors had sought. But his sentence, according to NOLA.COM , is less than federal sentencing guidelines of 57 to 60 months.
According to NOLA.COM , assistant U.S. Attorney Brian Klebba in making his argument to the judge to hold Keating’s sentence to two years said “when faced with a choice, Mr. Keating chose to admit to his misdeeds, forfeit his law license and tell the truth about the crimes that he and others committed.”
Keating must report to prison by January 11, 2027, according to the NOLA.COM reporting.
In its prepared statement announcing the sentencing, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Louisiana David Courcelle said in the plea from 2021, Keating admitted to paying fellow ringleader Damian Lebeaud for 31 tractor trailer crashes. Concurrently, Keating represented 77 plaintiffs involved in the staged collisions.
Lebeaud, like Keating, cooperated with prosecutors.His sentencing, like Keating’s, also has been delayed numerous times but is now set for December 3.
Keating’s attorneys on Friday requested that the U.S. Bureau of Prisons send Keating to the minimum-security satellite camp at FCI Beaumont Low. Keating, according to the court filing, suffers from “Common Variable Immunodeficiency (“CVID”) and also has two spinal cord stimulators.”
“Due to CVID and the spinal cord stimulators and his medication requirements, it is requested that he be designated to a Federal Medical Facility,” the filing said. The facility in Beaumont, Texas has the ability to treat those ailments, the attorneys said.
According to the U.S. Attorney’s office, payouts in the staged collisions totaled about $1.5 million for plaintiffs represented by Keating. He kept about $358,000 of that.

Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses.
The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield , a military version developed for the Pentagon.
While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military or the president. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
WHAT IS STARLINK?
Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
WHAT IS STARSHIELD?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarized version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programs has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported.
SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defense ministry has told Reuters.
Other U.S. partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.

This Mercedes-Benz Arocs Is a Bespoke Expedition Truck With a Comfortable Home Inside
13 photos
Photo: Motorcraft Adventure Developments
Heavy-duty, off-road trucks have carved out a niche in the overland landscape. While nimble mid-size trucks and SUVs have been the standard for outdoor exploration, more and more globetrotters are upgrading to heavy-duty commercial and military platforms for long-term journeys or even full-time living on the road.
Trucks like the MAN TGM and TGS, Mercedes-Benz Atego, Arocs, and Unimog provide an extremely robust foundation for capable expedition vehicles that can take you to any destination you have in mind. One of the companies turning big trucks into comfortable homes on wheels is Motorcraft Adventure Developments. If the name doesn’t ring a bell, know that this is a British manufacturer specializing in bespoke overland expedition vehicles, off-grid habitation units, and specialist commercial and military conversions.
The company’s builds prove that a rugged rig capable of conquering even the most inhospitable lands on our planet can also be incredibly comfortable and well-equipped for everyday living, and its latest Mercedes-Benz Arocs 4x4 expedition vehicle is a perfect example in this regard.
This massive overlander is built on a brand-new Mercedes-Benz chassis and is designed for long-distance travel and hassle-free off-grid living . The Arocs is an exceptional heavy-duty platform for this kind of round-the-world rig, providing the peace of mind you need when your plans involve expedition-style trips. Not only does it feature reinforced heavy-duty axles and multiple differential locks, but it also comes with specialized Modes like Rocking Free mode to escape sand, mud, or snow, and Crawler mode for slow-speed, technical maneuvers.
Photo: Motorcraft Adventure Developments More than that, it’s a highly adaptable chassis that can accommodate a voluminous habitation box, plus all the equipment needed for living on the road. Motorcraft outfitted it with a bespoke 18-foot (5.5-meter) habitation unit that is fully self-contained and completely separate from the driver’s cab.
The entire rig’s exterior is finished in metallic gray paint with black Raptor-coated cappings and is fitted with a series of accessories meant to make expedition trips easier. For instance, several fabricated side lockers provide useful storage space for tools, recovery gear, and other needed equipment, while a roof rack above the cab and habitation roof bars add even more equipment-carrying options.
At the rear, Motorcraft mounted a spare wheel and a hydraulic rear bike lift, which is a great addition for those who want to bring along motorcycles, bikes, of other expedition equipment . The truck rides on heavy-duty wheels with off-road tires, and it also comes equipped with hydraulic stabilizers.
What makes it even more impressive is the fact that all these components and every other essential product used in this rig’s construction is made by Motorcraft itself through its in-house accessories division, Motorcraft Overland Accessories.
Photo: Motorcraft Adventure Developments For the interior of this Arocs-based truck home, the British manufacturer took a residential approach. The generous habitation box allowed for a commodious open-plan living space that integrates all the essential functional zones you typically find in mobile homes, including a kitchen, a seating area, a sleeping space, and a bathroom.
The team furnished the space with handcrafted birch furniture, bamboo surfaces, and soft blue cabinetry, creating a contemporary interior that feels warm, bright, and inviting.
The layout puts the kitchen and a large U-shaped dinette in the center, with a fixed king-size bed at the rear and an enclosed bathroom at the front. The cooking area is equipped with an oven, an electric cooktop, a large stainless steel fridge and freezer, and a sink with a chrome tap. Plenty of under-counter and overhead cabinets provide storage for cookware and kitchen supplies, while bamboo worktops provide preparation space.
Next to the kitchen, the U-shaped dinette is slightly raised and offers a nice place to eat or relax. It features Alcantara upholstery and a handcrafted bamboo dining table, and the seating benches come with integrated storage. Several windows and rooflights bring natural light into the living area, while LED light strips illuminate the interior and create a nice ambiance in the evenings.
Photo: Motorcraft Adventure Developments There is no mention of whether the dinette can be converted into a bed, but the main sleeping area is just behind it and ready for use at any hour of the day. It’s flanked by windows for a nice cross breeze, and a wall-mounted TV provides entertainment. The entire upper section of the lounge and bedroom areas is lined with overhead cabinets, ensuring there is enough room for clothing, bedding, and other travel essentials.
As mentioned, there is no pass-through to the cab in this truck home. Instead, a full-width wetroom sits at the front of the habitation box . It is spacious enough for a mobile home and fitted with everything required for extended travel, including a shower, toilet, handheld shower system, heated towel rail, and mirror. It even integrates storage cupboards and a washing machine.
Photo: Motorcraft Adventure Developments Since this is a rig for year-round travel, providing comfort in any season was an important consideration. As such, the Arocs comes with roof-mounted air-conditioning, opening windows, and a diesel heater. The listing on Motorcraft’s website doesn’t mention the capacity of the water tanks or the solar system.
It does mention the pricing, though, and it’s a rather steep one. At £475,000 plus VAT (about $632,730), this Mercedes-Benz Arocs 4x4 truck home is definitely an overlander for the well-heeled.
Recently, Motorcraft Adventure Developments has expanded its operations across the Atlantic. The company has opened a Motorcraft USA facility in Saint George, Utah, which will bring its bespoke expedition vehicles to overlanding lovers in the United States.
